name: Modern Chaldean, dialect of Mangesh
catalog_citation: Sara, Solomon I. 1974. A Description of Modern Chaldean (Janua Linguarum, Series Practica 213). The Hague/Paris: Mouton [De Gruyter Mouton e-reprint 2017; Google Books preview id 4ZNsDwAAQBAJ, pg=PA22].
catalog_locator: p. 22, ch. 'Phonology', sec. 1.0 'Phonology of the word', a. 'Prosody of the word' (saved page image)
catalog_quote: The accent (stress) in Chaldean is cumulative and has no distinctive function. Its position is completely predictable. In monosyllabic words, it falls on the vocalic element irrespective of other features, and in polysyllabic words it regularly falls on the penultimate. It functions as the principal reliable phonological demarcative feature indicating word boundaries. /béθa/ 'house' /beθóxin/ 'your house'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (Google Books preview page image of Sara 1974, De Gruyter e-reprint). The page is headed PHONOLOGY / 1.0 PHONOLOGY OF THE word / a. Prosody of the word, and reads word for word: 'The accent (stress) in Chaldean is cumulative and has no distinctive function. Its position is completely predictable. In monosyllabic words, it falls on the vocalic element irrespective of other features, and in polysyllabic words it regularly falls on the penultimate. It functions as the principal reliable phonological demarcative feature indicating word boundaries. /béθa/ 'house' /beθóxin/ 'your house''. The quote is verbatim at the stated locator (p. 22, sec. 1.0a); is the end of the Introduction, confir…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and predictable: it falls on the penultimate syllable of any polysyllabic word (and on the only vowel of a monosyllable); suffixation moves it rightward so that it stays penultimate (béθa -> beθóxin).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in Sara; none of the other sources read describe a secondary-stress rule (Khan 2002 and Napiorkowska 2015 treat phrase-level 'stress groups'/nuclear stress instead).
new_statements.exceptions: Sara states none. Corroborating sources for sister Chaldean/Mosul-Plain varieties list exceptions: Khan 2002 (Qaraqosh, snippets pp. 67-68): pronominal object suffixes on verbs often ignored (k-ódilə), stress shifted to the final syllable in some verb forms (k-amaxwalhá), irregular stress in some loanwords, nuclear stress may move to the final syllable at the end of an intonation group (p. 471); Napiorkowska 2015 (Diyana-Zariwaw, p. 64): initial stress in vocatives (b-ʾálaha), 2pl pronoun ʾaxtū́n final, mádənxa 'East', enclitic copula/possessive suffixes do not count (brátela); Maclean 1895 §8: vocatives initial, 3pl-suffixed words and -a'it adverbs oxytone, 2pl suffix/pl. imperative antepenultimate, enclitics count as part of the word; Rhétoré 1912 §71 (older, divergent): claims final stress in consonant-final words (kthawan, chaklet) and penultimate in vowel-final words, foreign words keep their accent unless nativized.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for citation forms; Sara calls stress the demarcative signal of word boundaries. Khan 2002 ch. 6 and Coghill 2019 n. 7 describe phrase-level 'stress groups' (proclitic/enclitic combinations bearing a single stress, e.g. numeral + noun with stress shifted to the numeral's final syllable) and intonation-group-final shift of nuclear stress to the ultima in lively narrative/Gospel reading (Khan 2002: 471-473).
new_statements.identity_note: Sara 1974 describes 'Modern Chaldean' as spoken in Mangesh (Christian/Chaldean town in Dohuk province near the Turkish border, the author's native dialect), one of the dialects Glottolog groups under Chaldean Neo-Aramaic (chal1275). Corroborating first-hand statements read: Rhétoré 1912 (dialecte de la plaine de Mossoul = Alqosh/Telkepe area, chal1275 proper), Napiorkowska 2015 (Christian Diyana-Zariwaw, listed by Glottolog under chal1275), Khan 2002 snippets (Qaraqosh/Baghdede, Syriac-Catholic town whose dialect Glottolog also files under chal1275), Maclean 1895 (pan-NENA, Urmi-centred, i.e. mostly assy1241 but explicitly covering the 'Plain of Mosul'/Alqosh). All agree on regular penultimate word stress; only Rhétoré 1912 additionally claims final stress for consonant-final words, which the modern descriptions do not support.

sources.note: Stress is cumulative, non-distinctive, completely predictable: on the vowel in monosyllables, regularly on the penultimate in polysyllables; demarcative of word boundaries. Ex. /béθa/ 'house', /beθóxin/ 'your house'.

sources.note: p.64: 'The stress in nominals falls on the penultimate syllable both in the singular and the plural forms' (bráta, xabū́ša, qarqamyáte, betóxün); vocatives may take initial stress (Iranian substrate); enclitic copula/pronominal suffixes do not move stress off the nominal's penult; personal pronouns penultimate except 2pl ʾaxtū́n (final); p.66 (snippet) verbal stress likewise penultimate on the verbal base.

sources.citation: Rhétoré, Jacques. 1912. Grammaire de la langue Soureth ou Chaldéen vulgaire, selon le dialecte de la plaine de Mossoul et des pays adjacents. Mossoul: Imprimerie des Pères Dominicains. Chap. V 'Accent tonique', §§68-72, pp. 21-22.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: §70 monosyllables bear the accent; §71 polysyllables have the accent on the ultima or penult: on the ultima in words ending in a 'quiescent letter' (consonant), e.g. kthawan 'notre livre', chaklet 'tu prends'; on the penult in words ending in a vowel, e.g. Mara, malpani, taiboutha; proclitic groups (plit-oua-ly) take one accent on the penult of the group; §72 foreign words keep their own accent (ouâli) unless nativized (khadâma).

sources.note: 'In speaking the accent is almost invariably placed on the penultimate, even in foreign words.' Exceptions: vocatives on the first syllable; words with 3pl suffix often oxytone (esp. Urmi); adverbs in -a'it oxytone; some adverbs/particles on the first; 2pl suffix and pl. imperative often antepenultimate; affixes and enclitic verb 'to be' count as part of the word; Sal./Q./Gaw. plurals oxytone after loss of final syllable. Pan-dialectal (Urmi-centred, includes Alqosh 'Al.').
